title: Tight Generalization Bounds for Noiseless Inverse Optimization
claim: Different notions of mismatch between estimated and true objectives relate geometrically, and the consistent parameter set shrinks to a polytope around the truth.
layout: 2 panels side by side; left parabola curves, right polytope from intersecting strips
description: Two-panel schematic. Panel (a) shows two parabolic objective curves, a solid black one for the estimated parameters and a dotted brown one for the true parameters. They are shifted vertically so their optima align. Each curve has a dot at its minimizer, a_θ̂(s) and a_θ*(s). A red arrow joins the two minimizers and is labeled action-level mismatch. A black vertical arrow marks the set-level mismatch. A tall brown arrow marks the regret. Ellipses sketch level sets. Panel (b) is a 2-D parameter plane with axes θ2 and θ3. Dashed strip boundaries in blue, green, brown and yellow cross each other. Their intersection forms a pink polytope outlined in dark red, with the true θ* near its lower part. A dotted inscribed circle marks the incenter estimate θ̂_T^in. The eye goes first to the pink polytope and the labeled parabolas.
caption: (a) Relation between the set-level mismatch, the action-level mismatch, and the true suboptimality loss (regret). Since additive shifts do not affect the optimal actions, we shift the objective curves vertically so that their optimal values coincide. (b) Geometric intuition for tightness in the two-dimensional case θ = (1, θ2, θ3) for Theorem 3.2. Each demonstration induces an asymmetric strip constraint. abstract: Inverse optimization (IO) seeks to infer the parameters of a decision-maker's objective from observed context--action data. We study noiseless IO, where demonstrations are generated by a ground-truth objective. We provide a high-probability ${O}(\frac{d}{T})$ generalization bound for the induced action set, where $d$ is the number of unknown parameters and $T$ is the size of the training dataset. We strengthen this guarantee under additional conditions that ensure uniqueness of the chosen action, bringing our IO guarantees in line with best-arm identification results in the bandit literature. We further show that the ${O}(\frac{d}{T})$ rate is tight over all consistent estimators considered here, and extend the result to both instantaneous and cumulative regret. Notably, the resulting regret lower bound matches the corresponding upper bounds in the adversarial setting, indicating that the stochastic IO setting is effectively adversarial for the class of estimators studied here. Finally, we propose a parameter-free algorithm with lower per-iteration complexity than generic solvers. Experiments validate the predicted rates and illustrate the tightness of our bounds.
